items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I was working with Walter Carlos, not Walter Carlos, Walter Sear. Carlos of course was the other person.

ctx.x: Were they quite a bit larger than they are now I would imagine?

Well it rather looked like an old fashioned telephone switchboard. Because you really did put cables from one hole into another hole, and the whole thing was a complicated style of cables. I guess I was the first guy to do pop and/or jazz at least jazz flavored things, on the synthesizer. And it followed shortly after the synthesizer had been introduced, really, to recording by “Switched On Bach.” That was — of course, I can’t say that I mastered the synthesizer by any means. I was working with Walter Carlos, not…

Well I’ve noticed that one thing that we’ve been interested in here in doing these archival tapes is that we keep some of the earlier jazz stories and music alive for students and anyone watching. And it seems to be kind of a passion of yours that the early, some of the early keyboard styles. Is this something that you’ve liked from the beginning? Or did you come to it later on?
